name: Gujarat Sultanate
info: A late medieval sultanate of western India, ruled by the Muzaffarid dynasty from Ahmedabad, remembered for its trade, its navy at Diu and its Indo-Islamic architecture until Akbar annexed it in 1573.

facts.capital: Anhilwada Patan; Ahmedabad (from 1411); Champaner in the 16th century
facts.founder: Zafar Khan, titled Muzaffar Shah I
facts.predecessor: Tughlaq dynasty of the Delhi Sultanate

t: Zafar Khan, governor of Gujarat for the Tughlaq dynasty, made himself independent after Timur's invasion weakened Delhi and declared himself Sultan Muzaffar Shah I in 1407.
The sultanate's prosperity reached its height under Mahmud Begada, and its greatest extent under Bahadur Shah.
The Mughal emperor Akbar annexed Gujarat in 1573, and it became a Mughal subah.
dyk: Mahmud Begada's sobriquet Begada literally means the conqueror of two forts, probably after he took Girnar (Junagadh) and Champaner (Pavagadh).
ev: Zafar Khan declares himself Sultan Muzaffar Shah I and issues coins in his name
Ahmad Shah I succeeds and moves the capital from Anhilwada Patan to his new city of Ahmedabad
Fath Khan takes the throne as Mahmud Begada, who expands the kingdom in all directions
The Portuguese Empire wrests Diu from the sultanate in the Battle of Diu
Bahadur Shah ascends the throne and expands the kingdom
The Mughal emperor Humayun attacks Gujarat and briefly occupies it
Bahadur Shah is killed by the Portuguese while making a deal with them
Akbar annexes the Gujarat Sultanate and Muzaffar Shah III is taken prisoner to Agra

sections.foundation:
The Muzaffarid dynasty was founded by Zafar Khan, later Muzaffar Shah I. Richard M. Eaton describes him as the son of a "peasant convert to Islam". The 16th-century court historian Sikandar ibn Manjhu, in the Mir’āt-i-Sikandarī, says his family belonged to the Tank sect of Khatris; a Sanskrit poem written for Mahmud Begada traces the line from the Solar dynasty, and some historians such as Aparna Kapadia consider the Muzaffarids of Rajput status. His father Sahāran, titled Wajih-ul-Mulk, came from Thanesar.

In 1391 Sultan Nasir-ud-Din Muhammad bin Tughluq appointed Zafar Khan governor of Gujarat with the title Muzaffar Khan, and in 1392 he defeated the former governor Farhat-ul-Mulk at the battle of Kamboi and occupied Anhilwada Patan. After Timur's invasion devastated Delhi, he declared independence in 1394. His son Tatar Khan imprisoned him in 1403 and ruled briefly as Muhammad Shah I before being poisoned. Freed, Zafar Khan declared himself Sultan Muzaffar Shah I in 1407, took the insignia of royalty and issued coins in his name.
sections.socioeconomy:
The sultanate's revenue came chiefly from the land. In the crown districts the state demand was nominally one-half of the produce, gathered through village headmen, called Patel or mukaddam in the north and Desai in the south. In the tributary states the chief's share rarely exceeded one-third of the crop and rarely fell below one-sixth, supplemented by special cesses and trade and transit dues. Towards the end of the reign of Muzaffar Shah II the ministers farmed the revenue on contract, and the Mirăt-i-Áhmedi reports large increases in what the land yielded, followed by confusion.

Its ports gave it a place in the sea trade, and Mahmud Begada built a navy off the coast of Diu. The sultans built lavishly, above all in Ahmedabad, founded by Ahmad Shah I on the Sabarmati River and styled Shahr-i-Mu'azzam, "the great city". Its monuments include the Jami Masjid of 1423, Teen Darwaza, Bhadra Fort and the Dada Harir Stepwell, and Champaner, the 16th-century capital, survives as an archaeological park.
sections.military:
The sultanate fought its neighbours for most of its history. Ahmad Shah I put down a rebellion of his uncles led by Firuz Khan, repelled Hushang Shah of the Malwa Sultanate, and led expeditions into Malwa in 1419, 1420, 1422 and 1438; he defeated the Bahmani Sultanate and annexed Thana and Mahim. Muhammad Shah II forced the ruler of Idar to submit and took tribute from Dungarpur, but was driven back from Champaner in 1449. Ahmad Shah II defeated the Malwa sultan at the Battle of Kapadvanj, and Mahmud Begada took the forts of Girnar and Champaner.

In 1519 Rana Sanga of Chittor defeated a joint army of Malwa and Gujarat, later invaded Gujarat and plundered its treasuries; after his death the sultans recovered and sacked Chittor fort in 1535. The Portuguese took Diu in the Battle of Diu in 1509. The sultanate was, after the Bahmani Sultanate, the second state in the subcontinent to use firearms and gunpowder artillery extensively. Under Muzaffar Shah III its army drew free soldiers, mercenaries and enslaved men forced to fight from Africa and Asia, and many of its specialist warriors were Habshi, Africans.
sections.governance:
Gujarat was divided into the khálsah, the crown domain ruled directly, and tributary lands left under their former rulers in return for tribute in service or money. The tribute depended on the terms each chief had accepted, and was sometimes collected by military expeditions led by the king, called mulkgíri. Inside the tributary states justice and revenue were managed as under the Chaulukya kings.

The crown territory was divided into districts, sarkars, either assigned to nobles to support troops or kept as crown domains under paid officers called muktiă, who kept the peace and collected revenue with soldiers sent from Ahmedabad and fortified posts, thánás, under thánadárs. Each sarkar was split into parganáhs under an ámil or tahsildár. Ahmad Shah I ruled that when a district governor was a royal slave his accountant must be free, and the reverse, so each would check the other. The sultanate comprised twenty-five sarkars. Succession was often settled by the nobles, who raised and deposed sultans, and under Ahmad Shah III they divided the kingdom among themselves.
sections.impact:
The sultanate created a distinctive Indo-Islamic architecture in Gujarat, which took elements of the earlier Maru-Gurjara style into mihrabs, roofs, doors, minarets and facades. Its 15th-century buildings are known for paired, slender, richly carved minarets, drawing on the skills of local stone-carvers who had worked on Hindu temples; the "shaking minarets" of the Jama Mosque in Ahmedabad fell in an earthquake in 1819. Mosques such as the Jama Masjid at Champaner, the Sidi Bashir Mosque and the Sidi Sayyed Mosque, and the complex at Sarkhej Roza, which Mahmud Begada enlarged as a summer retreat, belong to this style, which anticipates Mughal mihrabs, minarets, jali screens and chattris.

The sultanate also produced a large Persian historical literature, from the Tarikh-i-Muzaffar Shahi to the Mirat-i-Sikandari, written soon after Akbar's conquest, and the Arabic Zafarul-Walih bi Muzaffar wa Alih by Hajji Dabir. Its wars shaped the balance of power among Malwa, Khandesh, the Bahmanis and the Rajput states.
sections.decline:
The sultanate came under attack from both the Mughals and the Portuguese. Humayun attacked Gujarat in 1535 and briefly occupied it, during which Bombay, Bassein and Daman passed to the Portuguese. Bahadur Shah regained his kingdom but was killed by the Portuguese on board a ship while making a deal with them in 1537. He left no son; after a disputed succession the nobles chose Mahmud Shah III, who struggled with nobles seeking independence and was killed by his servant in 1554. Under Ahmad Shah III the nobles divided the kingdom, and he was assassinated in 1561.

In 1573 Akbar annexed Gujarat and it became a Mughal subah. The last ruler, Muzaffar Shah III, was taken prisoner to Agra. He escaped in 1583 and with the nobles' help briefly regained the throne before Akbar's general Abdul Rahim Khan-i-Khanan defeated him in January 1584. He took refuge with Jam Sataji of Nawanagar State, whose forces fought the Mughals at the Battle of Bhuchar Mori in 1591. He finally killed himself when he was handed over to the Mughals.

summary: The Gujarat Sultanate, founded by Zafar Khan as Muzaffar Shah I after Timur's invasion weakened Delhi, ruled western India from Ahmedabad and Champaner. It prospered under Mahmud Begada and reached its widest extent under Bahadur Shah, left a rich Indo-Islamic architecture, and fell to Portuguese pressure and Mughal conquest, ending with Akbar's annexation in 1573.
references: J. Chaube, History of Gujarat Kingdom, 1458-1537 (Munshiram Manoharlal Publishers, 1975)
Georg P. Taylor, The Coins Of The Gujarat Saltanat (Royal Asiatic Society of Bombay, 1902)

pointDescs.1407: Zafar Khan declares himself Sultan Muzaffar Shah I and issues coins in his name.
pointDescs.1411: Ahmad Shah I succeeds, puts down his uncles' rebellion and moves the capital to Ahmedabad.
pointDescs.1429: Ahmad Shah's army defeats the Bahmani forces at Nandurbar; Thana and Mahim are annexed.
pointDescs.1443: Ahmad Shah I dies; Muhammad Shah II subdues Idar and takes tribute from Dungarpur.
pointDescs.1449: Muhammad Shah II is forced to retreat from Champaner.
pointDescs.1458: Mahmud Begada takes the throne and begins expanding the kingdom in all directions.
pointDescs.1509: The Portuguese take Diu in the Battle of Diu, late in the reign of Mahmud Begada, under whom the sultanate prospered most.
pointDescs.1519: Rana Sanga defeats a joint army of Malwa and Gujarat and later plunders Gujarat's treasuries.
pointDescs.1527: Bahadur Shah takes the throne and expands the kingdom.
pointDescs.1532: Under Bahadur Shah the sultanate reaches its greatest territorial extent.
pointDescs.1535: Humayun attacks and briefly occupies Gujarat.
pointDescs.1537: Bahadur Shah is killed by the Portuguese.
pointDescs.1554: Mahmud Shah III is killed by his servant amid struggles with the nobles.
pointDescs.1561: Ahmad Shah III, whose nobles had divided the kingdom, is assassinated.
pointDescs.1573: Akbar annexes Gujarat as a Mughal subah.
